title: Modes in context
description: Memorize the seven major-scale modes, characteristic degrees, vamps, and one-string offsets.

cards.front: What is a mode, and when does it exist?
cards.back: A scale type obtained by treating a different degree of a parent scale as the tonic. A mode exists only when its tonic is heard as the tonic. The same seven notes with a different tonic are a different sound.

cards.front: List the seven modes of the major scale with starting degree, formula, and characteristic degree.
cards.back: Ionian 1: 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 (the major scale). Dorian 2: 1 2 b3 4 5 6 b7 (natural 6 against b3). Phrygian 3: 1 b2 b3 4 5 b6 b7 (b2). Lydian 4: 1 2 3 #4 5 6 7 (#4). Mixolydian 5: 1 2 3 4 5 6 b7 (b7 against 3). Aeolian 6: 1 2 b3 4 5 b6 b7 (natural minor). Locrian 7: 1 b2 b3 4 b5 b6 b7 (b5).

cards.front: Which modes are already familiar, and how many are new?
cards.back: Ionian is the major scale and Aeolian is natural minor, so five modes are new.

cards.front: What are the two ways to build a mode?
cards.back: From the parent: D Dorian is C major starting on D (D E F G A B C) — notes only, not the sound. From the formula: D Dorian is D natural minor with the sixth raised. Compare against the parallel major or minor to hear what is distinct.

cards.front: How does each common mode differ from parallel major or minor on the same root?
cards.back: Dorian: natural minor with raised sixth. Phrygian: natural minor with lowered second. Lydian: major with raised fourth. Mixolydian: major with lowered seventh. Locrian: natural minor with lowered second and fifth.

cards.front: Which modes have a major third, which have a minor third, and why is Locrian rare?
cards.back: Major third: Ionian, Lydian, Mixolydian. Minor third: Dorian, Phrygian, Aeolian, Locrian. Locrian has ♭5, so its tonic triad 1 ♭3 ♭5 is diminished and cannot be a stable home.

cards.front: How is modal harmony different from functional harmony?
cards.back: Functional: V or V7 pulls to I through the leading tone; a cadence establishes the key. Modal: the tonic is established by repetition, a drone, or a vamp, and by stressing the characteristic degree. Functional resolution is weak or absent.

cards.front: Does playing the parent scale over a chord make a mode?
cards.back: No. The characteristic degree must be in a chord or a prominent melody note. Playing the parent scale alone does not make the mode.

cards.front: Give the typical vamp and color for Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, and Mixolydian.
cards.back: Dorian: Dm–G (i–IV); major IV holds the natural B. Phrygian: Em–F (i–♭II); F holds the ♭2. Lydian: F–G (I–II); G holds B, the ♯4 of F. Mixolydian: G–F (I–♭VII); F holds the ♭7 of G.

cards.front: Why is G–F–G likely Mixolydian?
cards.back: The chords avoid a strong V to I. The F chord is the cue: it contains the ♭7 of G.

cards.front: Give one-string half-step offsets for Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, and Mixolydian.
cards.back: Dorian 0 2 3 5 7 9 10 12. Phrygian 0 1 3 5 7 8 10 12. Lydian 0 2 4 6 7 9 11 12. Mixolydian 0 2 4 5 7 9 10 12.

cards.front: On string 4 (open D), which fret differs between D Dorian and D natural minor?
cards.back: Dorian frets 0 2 3 5 7 9 10 12 (D E F G A B C D). Natural minor uses fret 8 (B♭) instead of fret 9 (B).

cards.front: On string 6, what changes from E natural minor to E Phrygian?
cards.back: Phrygian frets 0 1 3 5 7 8 10 12. Only the second is lowered: F♯ (fret 2) becomes F (fret 1).

cards.front: From string 6 fret 1, how does F Lydian differ from F major?
cards.back: Lydian frets 1 3 5 7 8 10 12 13 (F G A B C D E F). F major uses fret 6 (B♭) instead of fret 7 (B). The fourth rises.

cards.front: On string 3 (open G), how does G Mixolydian differ from G major?
cards.back: Mixolydian frets 0 2 4 5 7 9 10 12. Fret 10 (F) replaces fret 11 (F♯).

cards.front: A Mixolydian: which parent major, and what are the notes from A?
cards.back: A is degree 5 of D major. Notes of D major from A: A B C♯ D E F♯ G.

cards.front: Write all seven modes of C major by starting notes.
cards.back: C D E F G A B; D E F G A B C; E F G A B C D; F G A B C D E; G A B C D E F; A B C D E F G; B C D E F G A.

cards.front: Spell A Dorian, B Phrygian, C Lydian, and D Mixolydian.
cards.back: A B C D E F♯ G; B C D E F♯ G A; C D E F♯ G A B; D E F♯ G A B C.

cards.front: Name the parent major for E Dorian, A Mixolydian, F♯ Phrygian, and B♭ Lydian.
cards.back: D, D, D, and F.

cards.front: Spell G Dorian by formula and confirm it equals F major from G.
How do you hear D Dorian on the guitar, not just list its notes?
cards.back: Loop Dm–G, play D E F G A B C D, land on D and on B over the G. The B over G is the characteristic natural 6.

cards.front: What happens if you change a G–F Mixolydian vamp to G–D?
cards.back: The F♯ in D pulls up to G like a leading tone. The sound becomes functional I–V in G major. Home is now confirmed by V to I, and F versus F♯ changes role.
